items.en: We have a lot of time.
We are eating bread and cheese.
The metro is on the left.
The hotel is on the right.
The park is in the city center.
I have a lesson on Thursday.
We are going to the cinema on Friday.
We rest on Saturday and Sunday.
On Sunday I'm going to grandma's.
The lesson starts at nine o'clock.
I wake up at seven o'clock.
The bus comes in five minutes.
We have lunch at two o'clock.

ka-a1-have.title: Having Things: მაქვს
ka-a1-have.pattern: მე მაქვს · შენ გაქვს · მას აქვს · ჩვენ გვაქვს · თქვენ გაქვთ · მათ აქვთ
ka-a1-have.explanation: For objects, 'to have' is მაქვს. Like მყავს (for people and animals), it is an 'inverted' verb: the owner is in the dative case, so 'he has' is მას აქვს, with მას (to him) rather than ის. The person is shown by the start of the verb: მ- (me), გ- (you), nothing (him/her), გვ- (us), and -თ at the end adds plural 'you/they'. Negate with არ before the verb: არ მაქვს.
ka-a1-have.fact: The same inverted pattern is used for feelings and wants in Georgian: 'I have', 'I want', 'I love' and 'I like' all put the person in the dative case.

dialogue.en: No, I don't. Nino has one.

ka-a1-want.title: Wanting: მინდა
ka-a1-want.pattern: მინდა · გინდა · უნდა · გვინდა · გინდათ · უნდათ
ka-a1-want.explanation: 'I want' is მინდა, built the same way as მაქვს: მინდა (I want), გინდა (you want), უნდა (he/she wants), გვინდა (we want), გინდათ (you want, plural/polite), უნდათ (they want). The wanted thing stays in its basic form: მინდა წყალი ('I want water'). რა გინდათ? is the polite 'What would you like?' you'll hear in shops and cafés.
ka-a1-want.fact: უნდა also means 'must' when it comes before another verb, so context tells you whether someone 'wants' or 'has to'.

ka-a1-love.title: Love and Like: მიყვარს, მომწონს
ka-a1-love.explanation: მიყვარს means 'I love' (people, places, food you really enjoy) and მომწონს means 'I like' (something pleases me). Both work like მინდა: the person goes first in the dative and the verb shows who: გიყვარს / მოგწონს (you), უყვარს / მოსწონს (he/she). With a plural subject the verb adds -თ: ბავშვებს უყვართ ('children love').
ka-a1-love.fact: Literally, მომწონს means 'it pleases me', which is exactly how Spanish 'me gusta' and Russian 'мне нравится' work too.

ka-a1-hungry.title: Hungry and Thirsty
ka-a1-hungry.explanation: Being hungry and thirsty are verbs in Georgian, again with the person at the front: მშია ('I am hungry'), გშია? ('are you hungry?'), მწყურია ('I am thirsty'). For eating and drinking, the present tense is ვჭამ ('I eat') and ვსვამ ('I drink'); the thing you eat goes in the dative, ending in -ს: ვჭამ ვაშლს ('I eat an apple').
ka-a1-hungry.fact: ხაჭაპური comes in many regional styles. The boat-shaped Adjarian version, from the Black Sea coast, is served with an egg and butter in the middle.

ka-a1-present.title: Present Tense: ვ- for 'I'
ka-a1-present.pattern: ვსწავლობ · სწავლობ · სწავლობს · ვსწავლობთ · სწავლობთ · სწავლობენ
ka-a1-present.explanation: Regular verbs mark the person with prefixes and endings. 'I' and 'we' start with ვ-; 'he/she' ends in -ს; 'we' and plural 'you' end in -თ; 'they' ends in -ენ. Example with 'study': ვსწავლობ, სწავლობ, სწავლობს, ვსწავლობთ, სწავლობთ, სწავლობენ. The same works for ვმუშაობ (I work), ვცხოვრობ (I live) and ვლაპარაკობ (I speak). The direct object takes -ს: ვკითხულობ წიგნს ('I read a book').
ka-a1-present.fact: Georgian has no separate 'I am reading' vs 'I read': one present form covers both, so ვკითხულობ can mean either.

dialogue.en: I work at a hospital. And you?

ka-a1-city.title: In Town: -ში (in), -ზე (on)
ka-a1-city.explanation: Location is shown by endings stuck onto the noun: -ში means 'in' (ქალაქი → ქალაქში, 'in the city') and -ზე means 'on' or 'at' (მაგიდა → მაგიდაზე, 'on the table'). Nouns ending in -ი lose it before these endings. To ask where something is: სად არის ბანკი? ('where is the bank?'). Useful words: ახლოს (near), შორს (far), მარცხნივ (on the left), მარჯვნივ (on the right).
ka-a1-city.fact: Tbilisi's metro opened in 1966 and has two lines.

dialogue.en: Excuse me, where is the pharmacy?

ka-a1-days.title: Days of the Week
ka-a1-days.pattern: ორშაბათი · სამშაბათი · ოთხშაბათი · ხუთშაბათი · პარასკევი · შაბათი · კვირა
ka-a1-days.explanation: Monday to Thursday are counted from Saturday: ორშაბათი ('two after Saturday'), სამშაბათი, ოთხშაბათი, ხუთშაბათი. Then პარასკევი (Friday), შაბათი (Saturday) and კვირა (Sunday, which also means 'week'). 'On Monday' adds -ს: ორშაბათს. 'Today' is დღეს, 'tomorrow' ხვალ and 'yesterday' გუშინ.
ka-a1-days.fact: Because კვირა means both 'Sunday' and 'week', ამ კვირაში means 'this week'.

ka-a1-time.title: Telling the Time
ka-a1-time.pattern: რომელი საათია? · რვა საათია · ცხრა საათზე
ka-a1-time.explanation: Ask რომელი საათია? ('what time is it?'). Answer with the number and საათი ('hour'): რვა საათია ('it's eight o'clock'). 'At' a time uses -ზე on საათი and the short number form: ცხრა საათზე ('at nine'), შვიდ საათზე ('at seven'). Numbers ending in -ი drop it before საათზე: შვიდი → შვიდ საათზე.
ka-a1-time.fact: საათი means 'hour', 'clock' and 'watch' — one word for all three.

dialogue.native: ათი საათია. გაკვეთილი თერთმეტ საათზე იწყება.
dialogue.en: It's ten. The lesson starts at eleven.
